content: Preeclampsia is defined as gestational hypertension accompanied by proteinuria of 300 mg or more over a 24-hour period. The pathophysiological abnormalities associated with preeclampsia include placental ischemia, generalized vasospasm, abnormal hemostasis with activation of the coagulation system, vascular endothelial dysfunction, altered nitric oxide and lipid metabolism, leukocyte activation, changes in various cytokines, and increased insulin resistance. It is crucial to identify individuals at high risk of developing preeclampsia during pregnancy to ensure better management. Maternal and fetal outcomes in preeclampsia are influenced by factors such as the gestational age at onset and delivery, the severity of the disease, the presence of multifetal gestation, and preexisting medical conditions like diabetes, renal disease, or thrombophilias. Preeclampsia is associated with an increased risk of placental abruption, preterm birth, fetal intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), acute renal failure, cerebrovascular and cardiovascular complications, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and maternal mortality. Early diagnosis is therefore essential. High-risk factors for preeclampsia include a history of hypertensive disorders in a previous pregnancy, maternal conditions such as chronic kidney disease, autoimmune diseases, diabetes, and chronic hypertension. Women are considered at moderate risk if they are nulliparous, aged 40 years or older, have a body mass index (BMI) of 35 kg/m² or higher, have a family history of preeclampsia, are carrying multiple fetuses, or have a pregnancy interval exceeding 10 years. Additional clinical factors associated with preeclampsia include elevated mean arterial blood pressure before 15 weeks of gestation, polycystic ovarian syndrome, sleep-disordered breathing, infections such as periodontal disease, urinary tract infections, and Helicobacter pylori, as well as vaginal bleeding for at least five days during pregnancy. The use of oocyte donation carries a higher risk of preeclampsia compared to in vitro fertilization (IVF) without oocyte donation or natural conception. Common causes of preeclampsia include uteroplacental ischemia and genetic predisposition. These may result from the formation of atheromatous plaques and fibrinoid necrosis in the spiral vessel walls, oxidative stress in trophoblast cells, apoptosis in trophoblast cells, systemic inflammatory responses, vasospasm, platelet aggregation, thrombin formation, and fibrin deposition in multiple organs. To manage preeclampsia effectively, low-dose aspirin should be initiated in women with two or more moderate risk factors. Women with a history of preeclampsia in a previous pregnancy should maintain a healthy weight and ensure that other conditions, such as diabetes, are well-controlled before conceiving. Once pregnant, these women should attend early and regular prenatal care visits. If a pregnant woman experiences symptoms such as swelling, severe headache, vision changes, or other signs of preeclampsia, she should contact her healthcare provider immediately. Adopting a healthy lifestyle, including maintaining a healthy weight, regular exercise, a well-balanced diet, and avoiding smoking and alcohol, is also important. Pregnant women should avoid taking any medications, vitamins, or supplements without consulting their healthcare provider first.
